q1.title: A cyclist’s ride
q1.intro: The speed–time graph shows a cyclist’s ride.

parts.q: Describe the motion of the cyclist between 10 s and 30 s.
pts: Constant (steady) speed
parts.model: She moves at a constant speed of 8 m/s.

q2.title: Colliding trolleys
q2.intro: Trolley A (mass 1.5 kg) moves at 4.0 m/s towards trolley B (mass 0.50 kg), which is at rest. They collide and stick together.

parts.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
pts: Total momentum before = total momentum after (when no external forces act)
parts.model: When no external forces act, the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after it.

parts.q: State two effects that a resultant force can have on a moving trolley.
pts: Change its speed
Change its direction
parts.model: It can change the trolley’s speed and it can change its direction.

parts.q: After the collision there is no friction. Explain why the trolleys keep moving at a constant velocity.
pts: There is no resultant force
parts.model: There is no resultant force on them, so their velocity does not change.

q3.title: A crane at work
q3.intro: A crane lifts a load of mass 600 kg through a height of 15 m in 30 s. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

parts.q: Name the energy store of the load that increases as it is lifted.
pts: Gravitational potential
parts.model: Its gravitational potential energy store.

parts.q: Suggest two reasons why the efficiency is less than 100%.
pts: Friction in moving parts
Energy heats the motor or surroundings
Sound is produced
Resistance of the wires heats them
parts.model: Friction in the moving parts wastes energy, and the motor and wires heat up, transferring energy to the surroundings.

parts.q: State the principle of conservation of energy.
pts: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
parts.model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is only transferred from one store to another.

q4.title: Boiling a kettle
q4.intro: An electric kettle heats 1.2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C.

parts.q: Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in liquid water.
pts: Close together (touching), irregular arrangement
Move past each other / randomly
parts.model: The particles are close together in an irregular arrangement, and they move around, sliding past each other.

parts.q: While the water boils, its temperature stays at 100 °C even though energy is still supplied. Explain why, in terms of particles.
pts: The energy is used to overcome the forces (bonds) between particles
So the kinetic energy of the particles (temperature) does not increase
parts.model: The energy is used to overcome the forces between the particles so they can separate into a gas, not to increase their kinetic energy, so the temperature stays the same.

parts.q: Explain why the heating element is at the bottom of the kettle.
pts: Heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises
Sets up a convection current so all the water is heated
parts.model: Water near the element expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler, denser water sinks to take its place, setting up a convection current that heats all the water.

q5.title: Sound and ultrasound
q5.intro: Sound travels through air at 340 m/s.

parts.q: Sound is a longitudinal wave. State what is meant by a longitudinal wave.
pts: Vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel
parts.model: The vibrations are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.

parts.q: State the range of frequencies that humans can hear.
pts: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
parts.model: About 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

parts.q: Describe the difference between a compression and a rarefaction.
pts: Compression: particles closer together (higher pressure)
Rarefaction: particles further apart (lower pressure)
parts.model: In a compression the air particles are pushed closer together; in a rarefaction they are spread further apart.

parts.q: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
pts: Sound needs a medium / particles to vibrate
A vacuum has no particles
parts.model: Sound is passed on by vibrating particles, and a vacuum contains no particles, so there is nothing to carry the vibrations.

q6.title: Light in glass
q6.intro: A ray of light passes into a glass block.

parts.q: Define the critical angle.
pts: The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°
parts.model: The angle of incidence at which the angle of refraction is 90°.

parts.q: Describe what happens to light inside the block when it hits the surface at more than the critical angle.
pts: Total internal reflection
All the light is reflected back inside; none leaves
parts.model: Total internal reflection: all of the light is reflected back into the glass and none passes out.

parts.q: A converging lens forms an image of a distant object on a screen. State two properties of the image.
pts: Real
Inverted
Diminished
parts.model: It is real, inverted and diminished.

q7.title: A resistor circuit
q7.intro: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a 6.0 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor in parallel.

parts.q: State what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
pts: The electrical work done (energy transferred) by the source
Per unit charge moved around a complete circuit
parts.model: The electrical work done by the battery in moving a unit charge around the complete circuit.

parts.q: State one advantage of connecting the lamps in a house in parallel.
pts: Each lamp can be switched on and off independently / others stay on if one fails / each gets the full p.d.
parts.model: Each lamp can be switched on and off on its own, and the others stay on if one breaks.

q8.title: Radioactivity and the Sun
q8.intro: A student investigates a radioactive source in the laboratory.

parts.q: State what an alpha particle consists of.
pts: Two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus)
parts.model: Two protons and two neutrons: a helium nucleus.

parts.q: State which type of radiation is the most penetrating.
pts: Gamma
parts.model: Gamma radiation.

parts.q: Name the nuclear process that releases energy in the Sun.
pts: Nuclear fusion
parts.model: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.

parts.q: State two precautions the student should take when handling the source.
pts: Use long tongs / keep a distance
Store in a lead-lined box / use shielding
Keep the time of exposure short
Point it away from people
parts.model: Handle the source with long tongs, and keep it in a lead-lined box when it is not being used.

parts.q: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted. State what this suggests about the Universe.
pts: The Universe is expanding (galaxies are moving away)
parts.model: The galaxies are moving away from us, so the Universe is expanding.

q9.title: A metal block
q9.intro: A rectangular metal block measures 0.20 m × 0.10 m × 0.050 m and has a mass of 2.7 kg. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

parts.q: Explain how the pressure changes if the block is stood on its smallest face.
pts: The pressure increases
The same force acts on a smaller area
parts.model: The pressure increases, because the same weight acts on a smaller area.

q10.title: Springs and see-saws
q10.intro: A student tests a spring, then balances a see-saw.

parts.q: Describe how the student finds the extension of the spring for a given load.
pts: Measure the original (unstretched) length with a ruler
Measure the new length and subtract the original length
parts.model: Measure the original length of the spring with a ruler, add the load, measure the new length, and subtract the original length from it.

parts.q: State what is meant by the limit of proportionality.
pts: The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to load
parts.model: The point beyond which the extension is no longer proportional to the load.

parts.q: State the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium.
pts: No resultant force
No resultant moment
parts.model: There is no resultant force and no resultant moment.

q11.title: Generating electricity
q11.intro: Countries use many different energy resources to generate electricity.

parts.q: Describe how electricity is generated in a gas-fired power station.
pts: Burning gas heats water in a boiler to make steam
The steam turns a turbine
The turbine turns a generator
parts.model: The gas is burned to heat water in a boiler, making steam. The steam turns a turbine, which turns a generator to produce electricity.

parts.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using solar cells.
pts: Advantage: renewable, no carbon dioxide, free fuel
Disadvantage: no output at night, unreliable in cloud, needs a large area
parts.model: Advantage: they are renewable and produce no carbon dioxide. Disadvantage: they produce no electricity at night.

parts.q: Name one energy resource whose energy does NOT come from the Sun.
pts: Geothermal, nuclear or tidal
parts.model: Geothermal energy.

q12.title: Gases and keeping warm
q12.intro: Particles, gases and thermal energy transfer.

parts.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.
pts: Particles collide with (hit) the walls
Each collision exerts a force on the wall
parts.model: The gas particles move randomly and collide with the walls; each collision exerts a force, and the force per unit area is the pressure.

parts.q: Explain why a white, shiny car stays cooler in sunshine than a dull black car.
pts: White/shiny surfaces reflect infrared radiation
Dull black surfaces absorb more infrared
parts.model: The white, shiny surface reflects most of the infrared radiation, while the dull black surface absorbs much more of it.

parts.q: Explain how the vacuum in a vacuum flask reduces energy transfer.
pts: A vacuum contains no particles
So conduction and convection cannot happen across it
parts.model: There are no particles in a vacuum, so energy cannot be transferred across it by conduction or convection.

parts.q: State what happens to the temperature of an object that absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.
pts: Its temperature increases
parts.model: Its temperature rises.

q13.title: Electromagnetic waves
q13.intro: Electromagnetic waves are used for communication.

parts.q: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum between infrared and ultraviolet.
pts: Visible light
parts.model: Visible light.

parts.q: State one use of microwaves and one danger of excessive exposure to them.
pts: Use: mobile phones, satellite TV, microwave ovens
Danger: heating of internal body cells
parts.model: Use: mobile phone signals. Danger: they can heat internal body cells.

parts.q: Give two advantages of digital signals over analogue signals.
pts: Data can be sent at a higher rate
Can be regenerated accurately, removing noise, so they travel further
parts.model: They carry data at a higher rate, and they can be regenerated accurately to remove noise, so they can travel further.

parts.q: Name the type of electromagnetic wave used to communicate with satellites.
pts: Microwaves
parts.model: Microwaves.

parts.q: Bluetooth uses radio waves. Suggest why the signal is weaker in the next room.
pts: The walls absorb or weaken the waves (and it is further away)
parts.model: Radio waves pass through walls but are partly absorbed, so the signal is weakened.

q14.title: Magnets, motors and induction
q14.intro: This question is about magnetic fields and electromagnetic effects.

parts.q: Describe how to use a small compass to plot the field lines around a bar magnet.
pts: Place the compass near the magnet and mark the direction the needle points
Move the compass along to the mark, repeat, then join the marks
parts.model: Put the compass near a pole and mark where the needle points with a dot. Move the compass so its tail is at the dot, mark again, repeat, then join the dots and add an arrow.

parts.q: A wire carrying a current between two magnetic poles feels a force. State what happens to the force if the current is reversed.
pts: The force reverses direction
parts.model: The force acts in the opposite direction.

parts.q: State two ways to increase the turning effect on the coil of a motor.
pts: More turns on the coil
A bigger current
A stronger magnet
parts.model: Use more turns on the coil and a larger current (or a stronger magnet).

parts.q: Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor.
pts: It reverses the current in the coil
Every half turn, so the coil keeps turning in the same direction
parts.model: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the forces keep turning the coil in the same direction.

parts.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. State two ways to increase the induced e.m.f.
pts: Move the magnet faster
Use a stronger magnet
Use more turns on the coil
parts.model: Move the magnet faster, or use a stronger magnet (or more turns).

parts.q: When the magnet is pulled out, the meter deflects the opposite way. Explain why.
pts: The induced e.m.f. opposes the change producing it
The change (the motion) is now reversed
parts.model: The induced e.m.f. always opposes the change that causes it. Pulling the magnet out is the opposite change, so the current flows the other way.

q15.title: A light sensor and a heater
q15.intro: A light sensor uses an LDR in a potential divider. A heater is plugged into the mains.

parts.q: State how the resistance of an LDR changes as the light intensity increases.
pts: It decreases
parts.model: Its resistance decreases.

parts.q: State why the switch of the heater must be in the live wire.
pts: So that switching off disconnects the heater from the live (high) voltage
parts.model: So that when it is switched off, the heater is disconnected from the live voltage and is safe.

parts.q: Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. State which fuse should be used and why.
pts: It is just above the normal current of 10 A
parts.model: 13 A, because it is the smallest rating above the normal current of 10 A.

parts.q: The heater has a metal case. Explain how the earth wire protects the user if the live wire touches the case.
pts: A large current flows to earth and the fuse melts
parts.model: A large current flows through the earth wire, so the fuse melts and disconnects the supply.

q16.title: Carbon-14 and the stars
q16.intro: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 5700 years.

parts.q: A nucleus of carbon-14 is written C-14 (proton number 6). State the number of protons and the number of neutrons.
pts: 6 protons
8 neutrons
parts.model: 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

parts.q: Describe what happens to a star like the Sun after it runs out of hydrogen.
pts: It expands into a red giant
It sheds a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf
parts.model: It expands to become a red giant, then throws off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf.

parts.q: State what is meant by a light-year.
pts: The distance light travels in one year
parts.model: The distance that light travels through space in one year.

parts.q: State what the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is evidence for.
pts: The Big Bang / the early, hot Universe that has expanded
parts.model: It is evidence for the Big Bang: radiation from the early Universe, stretched to microwaves as the Universe expanded.

a1.title: Stretching a spring
a1.intro: A student hangs loads on a spring and measures its length. The unstretched length is 12.0 cm.

parts.q: State the independent variable.
pts: The load (weight) on the spring
parts.model: The load on the spring.

parts.q: State one precaution to make the length readings accurate.
pts: Read the ruler with the eye level with the mark (avoid parallax) / use a set square or pointer
parts.model: Read the ruler with my eye level with the bottom of the spring, using a set square.

parts.q: Suggest two improvements to the experiment.
pts: Repeat each reading and take an average
Use more loads / a wider range
Use a pointer fixed to the spring / read at eye level
parts.model: Repeat each reading and average the results, and use more loads over a wider range.

a2.title: Resistance of a wire
a2.intro: A student measures the current through, and p.d. across, different lengths of a wire.

parts.q: State how the voltmeter should be connected to the wire.
pts: In parallel, across the wire
parts.model: In parallel with the wire, across its two ends.

parts.q: For lengths of 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm the resistances are 1.0, 2.0, 3.1, 3.9 and 5.0 Ω. Describe the relationship.
pts: Resistance increases as length increases
Resistance is (directly) proportional to length
parts.model: As the length increases, the resistance increases; the resistance is directly proportional to the length.

parts.q: The wire gets hot with a large current. Suggest how to prevent this.
pts: Use a small current / switch off between readings
parts.model: Use a small current and switch off between readings.

parts.q: Two students measure 5.0 Ω and 5.4 Ω for 100 cm of the wire. Do their results agree within experimental accuracy? Explain.
pts: Yes, they agree
The difference is 8%, which is less than 10%
parts.model: Yes. The difference is 0.4 Ω, which is 8% of 5.0 Ω, less than 10%.

parts.q: Suggest one source of error in this experiment.
pts: Difficulty placing the clips exactly / contact resistance / the wire heating up
parts.model: It is hard to place the crocodile clip exactly at each length, and the wire may heat up and change resistance.

a3.title: Cooling cans
a3.intro: A student compares how quickly hot water cools in a dull black can and a shiny silver can.

parts.q: Over 20 minutes, the temperature falls quickly at first and then more slowly. Describe the pattern shown by a graph of temperature against time.
pts: The temperature decreases
The rate of cooling decreases (the curve gets less steep)
parts.model: The temperature decreases, but the rate of cooling decreases over time, so the curve gets less steep.

parts.q: State two variables that must be kept the same for a fair comparison.
pts: Volume (mass) of water
Starting temperature
Room temperature / draughts
Size and shape of the cans
parts.model: The volume of water and the starting temperature.

parts.q: Predict which can cools faster, and explain why.
pts: The dull black can
Dull black is a better emitter of infrared radiation
parts.model: The dull black can, because dull black surfaces are better emitters of infrared radiation.

parts.q: Suggest two improvements to the experiment.
pts: Put lids on the cans
Insulate the bases
Stir before each reading
Use temperature probes and a data logger
Repeat the experiment
parts.model: Put a lid on each can to reduce cooling by evaporation and convection, and stir the water before each reading.

a4.title: Planning a pendulum investigation
a4.intro: A student plans to investigate how the length of a pendulum affects its period.

parts.q: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
pts: Independent: length of the pendulum
Dependent: period (time for one oscillation)
parts.model: Independent: the length of the string. Dependent: the period.

parts.q: State two control variables.
pts: Mass of the bob
Amplitude / angle of release
parts.model: The mass of the bob and the angle it is released from.

parts.q: Explain why the student should time 20 oscillations rather than one.
pts: It reduces the effect of reaction time
Divide by 20, so the error on each period is much smaller (more accurate)
parts.model: Reaction time causes an error at the start and end of timing. Over 20 oscillations, dividing by 20 makes that error much smaller for each period.

parts.q: Suggest a suitable number of lengths and a suitable range.
pts: At least five lengths
A sensible range, e.g. 0.20 m to 1.00 m
parts.model: Six lengths from 0.20 m to 1.00 m, in steps of about 0.15 m.

parts.q: State one safety precaution.
pts: Clamp the stand securely to the bench / keep clear of the swinging bob
parts.model: Clamp the stand firmly to the bench so it can’t fall over.
